# 88. Colour has roles, and the window follows the system appearance

Date: 2026-11-17

## Status

Accepted by Paul on 2026-11-17 (the merged plan, `docs/ux/UX_MERGED_PLAN.md`), implemented step by step: tokens and looks in U1, system theme, settings, menu and About in U2. **The number 88 was chosen by Paul on 2026-11-17**: it is the number the productivity line (84 to 89) left unused. Evidence: `docs/ux/UX_REVIEW.md`; tokens: `docs/ux/tokens.json` (equal to `crates/app/src/tokens.rs`, a test compares them).

## Context

The window draws every colour from `crates/app/src/theme.rs`, which is good, and then breaks its own rule in 56 places (`Color32` literals in `app.rs`, `tabs.rs`, `sheets.rs` and others). A review of `productivity-4-memory` against Apple's HIG (principles, read from the skill's reference pages) and the data-visualisation checks found:

* white on the dark accent is 3.21:1 (needs 4.5), the dark red is 2.98:1, control edges are 1.17 to 1.44:1 against their surface;
* the same colour carries several meanings (plum is brand, primary, selected and link; amber is running, stale and warning; there are two Compute buttons in two greens and plums), and up to four filled accent objects share one dark view, which is what makes the palette tiring;
* the top bar has its own Light/Dark button although Settings already has Follow system (HIG `dark-mode.md`: avoid an app-specific appearance setting);
* the viewport is always near-black, and its 12-colour domain palette fails the validator (adjacent colour-blind separation 4.3, floor 6).

## Decision

* **Colour is a set of roles, not values.** `crates/app/src/tokens.rs` holds every role in a light and a dark value as plain data (the table of `docs/ux/tokens.json`: page, card, raised, separator, control edge, text, muted, accent, on-accent, tint, activity, success, danger, canvas, chip); `theme.rs` turns it into the two `Visuals` and the role functions the window calls.
* **One colour, one meaning.** Accent = the primary action, links, focus and the selected-item bar. Activity (amber) = time and attention: running, queued, stale. Success and danger = outcomes. Data colours = plots and the canvas only.
* **Quiet by default.** At most one filled accent object per view (Compute). Selection is a tint with a 2 px accent bar. Neutral surfaces carry OKLCH chroma <= 0.026; the plum character lives in the text colour, the accent, the tint, the logo and the italic titles.
* **Text on fills follows the fill.** The brand pink is kept (Paul, 2026-11-17): plum `#820C4F` with white text in the light look, `#D96AA4` with ink text in the dark look (white on that pink is 3.21:1 and fails, ink is 5.62:1). Amber is a fill with ink text, and as text on light it is `#6B4300` on its tint.
* **Nothing by colour alone.** Every state shows a glyph and a word beside its colour.
* **Contrast is tested, not reviewed.** `theme.rs` has a unit test with the table of (foreground, background, minimum) pairs of the tokens: 4.5 for text, 3 for control edges, and fails when a token moves out of range. Control edges and separators are different tokens.
* **The window follows the system appearance.** The default is `ThemePreference::System`, applied live with `Context::set_theme` and `set_visuals_of` for the two sets; the top-bar Light/Dark button is removed; Settings keeps Follow system / Light / Dark.
* **The canvas is dark by default, in both looks** (decision D2); Settings can make it follow the look. Regions are drawn opaque with the validated eight colours of `tokens.json` (checked with all pairs, colour-blind and normal vision), every region carries a number chip and a legend row, and beyond eight the same hues are hatched (9 to 16) and then grey with the number (17 and more).
* **Settings: Theme (follow the system by default), Contrast (follow system, standard, high), Reduce motion, Canvas, Colour regions by.** High contrast is read from Windows (`SPI_GETHIGHCONTRAST`, one small FFI call) and is a setting everywhere; zoom set with Ctrl and +/- is kept.
* **One table of actions, two views** (`crates/app/src/menu.rs`): the command palette and the native menu bar list the same actions. The menu is native through `muda` (a new dependency, Windows only for now: it is the platform menu, so it is keyboard-, screen-reader- and High-contrast-correct without drawing it ourselves; the keys stay handled by the window). Linux (GTK) and macOS (main thread) are not tried yet: they keep the palette.

## Not in this decision

* **Type scale, control sizes (28 px), keyboard map and copy** (plan U2 and U3): they follow the same review and need no ADR of their own; the type scale and the 28 px control height are set in `theme.rs`.
* **Blur and translucent materials.** Rejected: egui does not draw them and the HIG limits them to a floating functional layer nyx does not have.
* **A user-editable palette or accent colour.** Not now; the roles make it possible later.
* **Pixel-exact screenshot tests.** The scripted shots are for review and a smoke test, not goldens.
decisions.title: Colour has roles, and the window follows the system appearance

# 89. Command lists are a front-end: checked, planned and run

Date: 2026-11-16

## Status

Accepted as a step of the productivity plan (S1, `docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md` section 3b). **Number 89: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.** Amends ADR 57 (front-ends are thin over `Engine::call`) with a third front-end; the scripting language of step S4 will extend this record, not replace it. **Built on** the queue (ADR 87) and on P0's command lists and the power-throttling opt-out (ADR 11 note, `process.rs`): the S1 bookmark is a merge of those lines.

## Context

An agent that wants a workflow (open, change a width, solve, read the index, five times) makes one tool call per command and finds a wrong argument at the call that uses it, perhaps an hour into a run. A person who wants the same workflow again has nothing to re-run. P0 wrote the workflows as JSON lines of `{cmd, args}` for timing; the same files are the smallest useful script.

## Decision

* **A command list is a file of JSON lines, `{"cmd": <command of Engine::catalog()>, "args": {...}}`**, sent to `Engine::call` in order. It is not a second model format and not a language: no loops, no values carried from one line to the next (the replay keys `job_arg`, `after_stage`, `delay_s`, `expect_error` and `note` exist for the cancel workflows and the timing tables). Blank lines and `#` lines are skipped. A language comes with step S4.
* **Three stages, the first two before anything runs** (`nyx_engine::commandlist`): *parse* (every line is an object with a `cmd` and known keys); *static* (the command is in the catalog, with a did-you-mean when it is not, and `args` fit its JSON Schema: type, enum, `oneOf`, required, no unknown argument; a keyword the checker does not know is not checked, so a valid command is never refused); *plan*, a dry run on a scratch copy of the engine in which every command that changes the project is applied for real and the commands that start work are only counted. The plan finds what only the project can tell (a solve with no physics at that point, a feature that does not exist, a problem that does not check, a result read before anything solves it) and says how many meshes and solve jobs the list would make, with the meshes the stage cache would reuse (ADR 87). It meshes nothing, solves nothing, writes nothing and starts no job. A bad line is reported with its line number and command and nothing runs; every problem of the static stage is reported at once.
* **Run** sends the lines to an engine in order, through the same commands the window and the MCP server use, so a solve waits in the queue like any other. It stops at the first failing command and at a replay key that cannot be honoured (a cancel that found no running job, an `expect_error` line that succeeded), so a step that did not happen cannot pass.
* **Front ends.** `nyx check FILE` prints the plan (`--json` for an agent), exit 2 on a problem; `nyx run FILE` checks and then runs (`--no-check` to skip the check, `--workspace DIR` to record every solve as a run of a workflow there, `--json` for one JSON line per command); exit 1 when a command fails. The `workflow` example replays through the same `run`.
* **The reference is generated from the same catalog** (`nyx_engine::apiref`, S2): `docs/api/` holds one page per command (title, access, description, a table of the arguments flattened from the JSON Schema with their types, required flags, defaults and the unit or meaning the schema states, and an example line made from the schema that passes `nyx check`) and an index; `nyx api list` and `nyx api show COMMAND` print the same text. A test regenerates the pages and fails when `docs/api/` differs, so the reference cannot disagree with a command, and another requires every argument to have a description. Rewrite after a deliberate change with `NYX_WRITE_API=1 cargo test --release -p nyx-engine --test api_docs`.
* **Where the logic lives.** In `nyx-engine` (`commandlist.rs`), with the window and MCP server free to use it later; the app crate only parses arguments and prints (`runfile.rs`).

## Not in this decision

* **A script language, values between lines, loops, the run record holding the script text** (steps S4 to S6). A list says what to do, not what to do next.
* **Cost estimates in the plan** (plan Q2): the plan counts meshes and solves and does not say how long they take.
* **Planning commands that read results** (`result_info`, `analyse`, ...): they are checked for a result to read, not run.
* **`open_results` in a plan**: it replaces the project with a file's, so the lines after it are checked without the checks that need to know what was solved.

## Consequences

* The P0 workflows are the first lists and are checked by a test (every list checks clean and the check starts nothing).
* `Engine::sweep_prepare` is the check of a sweep without submitting it, shared by `sweep_run` and the plan.
* No contract changes: the commands are the catalog's.

## Code

`crates/nyx-engine/src/{commandlist,apiref,sweep}.rs`, `crates/app/src/{runfile,apicmd,main}.rs`, `docs/api/`, `crates/nyx-engine/examples/workflow.rs`; tests `crates/nyx-engine/tests/{commandlist,api_docs}.rs`, `crates/app/tests/cli.rs`.
decisions.title: Command lists are a front-end: checked, planned and run

# 9. Every kernel is three stages behind one entry point

Date: 2026-11-03

## Status

Accepted (commits `fa6eff2`, `106e7f8`; table in `docs/KERNEL_PORT_STATUS.md`).

## Context

Kernels were single functions from mesh and spec to result. Swapping a linear-algebra backend (ADR 8), reusing an assembled system across a sweep, or exposing per-cell fields all required cutting them open.

## Decision

* `solve(mesh, spec, state)` / `solve_with(.., progress)` is the **one entry point for all physics**: it checks the element order and numbers (`validate`), dispatches by `Physics` (and by mesh dimension for EM waves), refuses a result containing NaN or infinity, and appends the plain-language stage log to `SolveResult::log`. A cancelled solve returns `Err("cancelled")`.
* Every kernel is **assemble -> solve -> fields**, and `solve_*` is their composition:
  1. *assemble*: matrices on the free dofs, constraints, loads, the material data later stages need;
  2. *solve*: the raw result (complex eigenpairs, a vector, transient states); the backend is chosen here (`spec.solver`, or the eigensolver the stage calls);
  3. *fields*: plot fields (node-averaged, as before) and `Solution::cell_fields`, the same quantities per cell and local node, not averaged, with wafer names and complex values where the quantity is complex.
* The node average of a cell field is the plot field of the same name (checked on every golden case).
* Splitting changed no number: the golden files are unchanged.

## Consequences

* A `femcore::solvers` adapter replaces one function per kernel.
* Stage function names are public API (`assemble_modes`, `solve_mode_pairs`, `mode_fields_cells`, ...); they are listed in contract `kernel_stages` because renaming one silently breaks callers outside the repository.
* The `Physics::Emw` dispatch by mesh dimension is a quiet rule (R10).
* `progress` is a thread-local, so stage functions called outside `solve_with` run unobserved and uncancellable (R19).

## Code

`crates/femcore/src/solve.rs`, `validate.rs`, `progress.rs`, `fields.rs`, and the kernels `dfs.rs`, `ems.rs`, `ems_pml.rs`, `ems_axisym.rs`, `ems3d.rs`, `sms.rs`, `sms_pml.rs`, `sms_floquet.rs`, `sms_lrb.rs`, `sms_kz.rs`, `sms_axisym.rs`, `sbs.rs`, `sbs_ring.rs`.

## Contract

`contracts/kernel_stages`: `crates/femcore/tests/stages.rs` (composition equals the one-call solver) plus `contracts.rs::kernel_stage_api_is_public`, which names every *public* stage function so removing one fails to compile. The stages of plain `sms`, `sms_lrb` and `ems3d` are `pub(crate)` (R26), so only 7 of 10 kernel families are reachable from outside the crate.
decisions.title: Every kernel is three stages behind one entry point

# 90. Whole-array operations on results are engine commands over a typed expression tree evaluated in Rust

Date: 2026-11-17

## Status

Accepted as step S3 (plan item N1) of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3b). **Number 90: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.** This record covers level N1 (whole-array operations) and the tree that levels N2 to N4 build on; N2 (text formulas, material values, `where`, vectors) is added below (step S5); N2b (tensor entries, a wavelength, a weight, boundary integrals) is step S5b; N3 (tracing script functions) is step S6, added below; N4 (a code generator) amends it if it lands.

## Context

A researcher or an agent wants numbers computed from a field: the integral of `|E|^2` over the core, the confinement factor, the largest stress, the field along a line, the overlap of two modes. Before this step the only way was `result_field`, which returns up to 2000 sampled node-averaged values, and a loop of arithmetic written by the caller. In an interpreted script such a loop is 10 to 100 times slower than Rust and, worse, it reads values that were averaged over the cells and sampled, so the number it gets is not the integral of the field the solver made.

## Decision

* **Eight commands, one implementation** (`nyx_engine::reduce`): `field`, `field_op`, `integrate`, `extremum`, `probe`, `line_cut`, `overlap` and `confinement`. They are ordinary engine commands (read access), so the MCP server lists them as tools, a script (S4) calls them, and the window's Reduce form in the Results tab calls the very same commands (`App::reduce_now`; the test compares the line it shows with the command's number).
* **A handle is a value, not an id.** `field` returns `{"field": "Ex", "physics": "ems", "solution": 0}`; arithmetic builds `{"op": "mul", "args": [a, b]}` (`add sub mul div neg abs abs2 re im conj sqrt pow`); numbers are `{"num": x}` or `{"num": [re, im]}`; a bare string is a field of the request's `physics` and `solution`. The engine keeps no handle table, so a handle has no lifetime and cannot go stale in the engine: it is read against the stored result each time and the answer says `stale` and `age_s` (as `result_field` does). The tree is `femcore::fieldexpr::Tree` (complex values, leaves are numbered slots, every operation written out so the order of the floating-point operations is fixed by that file).
* **A leaf reads the field the solver made.** A name is first looked up among the per-cell fields of the solution (`cell_fields`: `Ex`, `uz`, ..., complex when the solve is, not averaged over cells), then among the node-averaged flat fields of `result_info` (`T`, `|E|`: real, one value per dof). Both are Lagrange P1 or P2 interpolants on the cells of the mesh the result was solved on. **A stored result keeps that mesh** (`Stored.model`), so a result is read on its own cells whatever the project's mesh is now (a changed element size makes the result stale, not unreadable).
* **The rule (what N2, N3 and N4 must reproduce bit for bit).** Integrals use the degree-4 symmetric rule of `femcore::fem::quad_rule` (6 points on a triangle, 14 on a tetrahedron), exact for the product of two P2 fields; an integrand of higher degree carries the quadrature error. At each point every leaf is `sum_a N_a(q) v_a` (local node order, starting from 0.0) and the tree is evaluated on those values. A cell adds `vol * sum_q (w_q * f_q)`; cells are summed in blocks of 2048 consecutive cell numbers in cell order and the blocks in block order, so the sum has the same bits for any thread count (`tests/reduce.rs` runs it on 1, 3 and the pool's threads). The reference loops in `tests/reduce.rs` are written on the raw arrays of the result and agree **to the bit** with the commands; the closed forms (polynomials of degree 2 integrated by Gauss-Legendre over boxes) agree to 1e-9.
* **Measure.** The plane measure (area in 2D, volume in 3D) is the default. `revolution: true` multiplies the integrand at each quadrature point by `2 pi r` (r is mesh axis 0, the mesh must be 2D) for bodies of revolution. It is an explicit argument, echoed in every answer, because the engine does not know which physics is axisymmetric; when a result's study name says `axisym` and the argument is absent, the answer carries a note.
* **Maxima are nodal.** `extremum` takes the largest or smallest real value at the nodes of the cells of a region (vertices, and edge midpoints of a P2 mesh), not over the interpolant; it says so, and returns the cell, the local node and the point. A complex expression has no order and is refused with the advice to wrap it in `abs`, `abs2`, `re` or `im`.
* **`probe` and `line_cut`** find the cell of a point with a uniform grid of the cells' boxes and interpolate in that cell. Points are in mesh axes (a 2D mesh: x then z of the wafer; 3D: x, y, z). A point outside the mesh answers `inside: false` and a null value, not an error; a point on the face between two cells is read in the cell with the lowest number (the fields are not averaged, so the two cells can differ by the discretisation error).
* **`overlap` and `confinement` have no material weight.** `overlap` returns the complex integral of `sum_k conj(a_k) b_k` over a region, the two norms and the coefficient `|overlap|^2 / (norm_a norm_b)` (0 to 1, Cauchy-Schwarz); `a` and `b` are a field or a list of components. `confinement` returns the integral of `sum_k |c_k|^2` over a region divided by the same over the whole mesh. The energy or power fraction needs the permittivity at each point, which is N2 (material values in formulas); until then the commands say what they computed in `meaning`.
* **Where the tree lives.** The plan says N1's handle arithmetic builds the formula tree of N2, extending `femcore::expr`. That evaluator is real-valued and has no fields; making it complex and giving it field leaves is the substance of N2. So S3 adds the typed tree `femcore::fieldexpr` (complex, field leaves) and N2 adds a text parser that produces the same tree and moves `expr::Expr` (initial values from `x y z`) onto it. Until then there are two small evaluators in `femcore`; the gate for N2 is that a formula and a handle give the same bits.

## N2: text formulas (step S5, 2026-11-18)

A string in an `expr` is now a formula: `abs(Ex)^2 * eps_r`, `where(z > 0, p, 0)`, `inner(E, E)`. `femcore::formula` parses it once into the same `fieldexpr::Tree` that handles build, so a formula and a handle are one request with one evaluator, and the gate is that they give the same bits (`tests/reduce.rs::a_formula_equals_the_handle_form_to_the_bit`: `abs(Ex)^2 + abs(Ez)^2` equals the handle `add(pow(abs Ex), pow(abs Ez))`, and `Ex * Ez` equals `mul`, both to the bit; the loop on the raw arrays agrees).

* **Grammar** (the module comment of `formula.rs` is the reference): numbers (`2j` is imaginary), `pi`, `e`; `+ - * / ^` (also `**`), comparisons, `and or not`; `abs abs2 re im conj sqrt exp sin cos arg` on complex values; `log log10 tan sinh cosh tanh atan step min max atan2` and a non-integer power on real values; `where(cond, a, b)`, which evaluates only the branch that applies (so `where(x != 0, 1/x, 0)` is safe). A power with a whole constant exponent from -16 to 16 is repeated multiplication, which is exactly what the handle `pow` builds. Nothing else parses: no input can run code, name a file or call anything not listed. Nesting is limited to 64 levels.
* **Real-only operations are checked, not guessed.** `Tree::check` runs once per request, before any point, and refuses a comparison, a `where` condition, `log`, `tan`, `min` and so on whose operand is complex, naming the formula and advising `abs`, `abs2`, `re` or `im`. A formula never silently takes the real part.
* **Names** are resolved by the engine (`reduce::Namer`) in this order: the coordinates `x y z` (wafer axes; `y` is 0 on a cross-section; interpolated from the nodes like a field); a field of the result (a plain string that is exactly a field name still means that field, as before; a name that is not an identifier, such as `|E|` or `Re Ex`, goes in backticks inside a formula); a vector (`E` when the solution has two or three of `Ex Ey Ez`; `dot`, `inner` which conjugates the first, `cross`, `norm`, `norm2`, `E.x`); a **material value** by descriptor name (`eps_r`, `rho`, ...; `eps` and `mu` mean `eps_r` and `mu_r`). `material("rho")`, `region("Si")` and a backticked `ems:1:Ex` say what they are when a name is ambiguous or belongs to another physics or solution. An unknown name lists the names there are.
* **Material values are what the solver read.** They come from the problem of the physics as `nyx_physics::decode::materials_by_label` builds them for the solve (library materials, inline numbers, the optical model at the wavelength of the study), one scalar per cell, **constant over the cell** (not interpolated, so a region indicator or a material is the same number at every quadrature point). They are read from the project's current problem and the result's own mesh: if the materials changed since the solve the answer carries `stale: true`. A property that is a tensor in some material of the mesh (an anisotropic or rotated `eps_r`) is refused rather than read as its scalar default. `region("name")` is 1 in the cells of the region and 0 elsewhere.
* **An expression of numbers only** (`1`, for an area) uses the mesh of the default result.
* **`femcore::expr` is unchanged.** The plan says N2 moves `expr::Expr` onto the new tree. It does not: `expr` is the real grammar of geometry and initial fields that `geom::expr` copies (ROUGH_SPOTS R06), the two are held equal by `tests/expr_grammar.rs`, and moving one side would break that test or force `geom` onto `femcore`. The formula grammar is a superset kept separate, and the gate "the existing `expr_grammar` tests unchanged" holds because the file is untouched. Two evaluators remain in `femcore`: the real one for geometry and initial fields, the typed one for results.
* **Not done in S5, built in N2b below:** line and surface integrals; tensor material values; a material dispersion at another wavelength. Still not done: a formula inside a worker.

## N2b: tensor entries, a wavelength, a weight, boundary integrals (step S5b, 2026-11-19)

What S5 left out, built on the same tree. The formula box of the Reduce form (Results tab) is a text field whose content goes to `integrate` and `extremum` unchanged, so the window and a script give the same number.

* **Tensor entries.** A tensor property has plain names for its entries in wafer axes: `eps_r_xx`, `eps_r_yy`, `eps_r_zz`, `eps_r_xy`, `eps_r_xz`, `eps_r_yz` (and `k_*`, `alpha_*`; `eps_zy` is `eps_r_yz`; `eps` and `mu` keep meaning `eps_r` and `mu_r`). The entries come from `Materials::cell_tensor`, the call the solvers make, with the crystal orientation applied, so an isotropic material is `v I` and a mesh with both kinds reads correctly. The frame is the global (wafer x, y, z) one of `cell_tensor`; `section::local_tensor`, which reorders to (x, z, y) for the kernels, is not used. The plain `eps_r` is still refused on a mesh where some material is a tensor, and its message names the entries. Gate: r-plane sapphire at 57.6 degrees (a non-zero yz entry), every one of the nine entries equals the library's `optical_permittivity` for the same angles to 1e-9 of the area-weighted value.
* **`wavelength`** (metres), an optional argument of every reduction: where the material values of a dispersive model are read, default the study's. The fields stay those of the solve; it is an explicit what-if on the materials, not a re-solve. The leaf records it, so two wavelengths in one formula are two leaves.
* **`weight`** of `confinement`: a real formula that multiplies the integrand (`eps_r` gives the energy fraction). Without it the tree, and so the bits, are those of S3; with it the answer equals the ratio of two `integrate` calls to the bit.
* **Boundary integrals** (`integrate` with `boundary`, in place of `region`). Decisions:
  * Only named boundaries: an outer boundary (the labelled facets of the solver mesh, edges in 2D and triangles in 3D, by `LabelResolver::boundaries`, the same text the conditions use), or an interface `a|b` between two regions. The solver mesh keeps no facets for an interface, so for a name that reads `a|b`, has no facets and whose two parts are regions, the faces are those shared by a cell of `a` and a cell of `b`, which is what the geometry names `a|b` (all its pieces). An arbitrary path or surface is not integrated; `line_cut` samples a line.
  * **An interface has two sides and the fields are discontinuous across it** (`Ex`, `eps_r` at Si/SiO2). A facet with two adjacent cells needs `side`, a region name: the facet is read in its cell that belongs to the region, and the answer says which side. A facet with one cell (an outer boundary) needs none; a facet with two cells and no `side`, or with both cells in `side`, is an error that names the boundary. Nothing picks the lowest-numbered cell.
  * **The normal** `nx`, `ny`, `nz` (wafer axes, unit length, constant on a facet) points out of the chosen cell. These names exist only in a boundary integral and are an error elsewhere. A flux is `dot(F, [nx, ny, nz])`.
  * Rule: the facet rule of `fem::facet_rule` (3-point Gauss on an edge, degree 5; the degree-4 triangle rule on a face); each point is mapped to the barycentric coordinates of the chosen cell, where the leaves are interpolated exactly as in a volume integral. A facet adds `measure * sum_q (w_q f_q)`; facets are summed in blocks of `BLOCK` consecutive facets in facet order, so the bits do not depend on the thread count.
  * `revolution` is supported on a 2D (r, z) mesh: the integrand and the measure are multiplied by `2 pi r` at each point. The answer reports `measure` (length, area; with `revolution` the surface of revolution) and the number of facets.
  * Gates: the length of a known boundary (expr `1`) and the area of one in 3D; a closed form on a uniform field (flux through a face is `F . n A`); the divergence theorem on a smooth field: the integral of `dot(F, n)` over the whole outer boundary equals the area integral of `div F`.

## N3: a script function becomes a formula (step S6, 2026-11-19)

`nyx.integrate(expr=integrand, region="Si")` with `def integrand(p): ...` calls `integrand` **once**, with a symbolic point, records what it does as formula text, and sends that text to the engine, where it is the N2 formula of the same words. Nothing new reaches the engine: no command, no argument, no change to `engine_commands`. The traced function is a way to *write* a formula, so the bit-identity gate of N2 carries over unchanged: the engine sees text and parses it with the one parser.

* **Where it runs.** In the script worker, as Python (a prelude fed before the user's script, generated by `nyx_script::trace::prelude` from `Engine::catalog()`). Monty runs the function, so loops with a fixed number of steps, helper functions, comprehensions and local variables all work, as in JAX. The function is called once per command, not per element (a counter in the test says 1).
* **The symbolic value** is an instance of a small class `Sym` that holds formula text. `+ - * / **`, unary minus, `abs`, and their reflected forms build text with **every operation parenthesised and operand order kept** (`2 * e.x` is `(2 * E.x)`, never `(E.x * 2)`; `1 - e.x` is `(1 - E.x)`), so the parsed tree is the tree of the same expression written by hand (the parser makes no node for a parenthesis). A number is written with Python's `repr` (shortest text that reads back as the same double; an integer stays an integer, so `x ** 2` stays the repeated product the parser makes of `^2`). A bool is 1 or 0; a number that is not finite, a complex number or any other value (text, a list) is an error that says what a traced function computes with.
* **The argument of the function** is one value, `p`, the point: `p["E"]` is the vector field `E` (components `.x .y .z` are `E.x`, ...), `p["eps_r"]` a material value, `p["Ex"]` a field, `p["nx"]` a normal; `p.x p.y p.z` are the coordinates. `p["name"]` is a name of a formula; the engine resolves it, so an unknown name gets the engine's own message listing the names there are. **Deviation from the plan** (`def integrand(e, eps)`): Monty gives a function no `__code__` and no `inspect`, so a parameter cannot be bound by its name; the plan's form is one `p` with names as keys.
* **Functions** are the prelude's: `where(c, a, b)`, `sqrt exp sin cos log log10 tan sinh cosh tanh atan atan2 step re im conj arg abs2 minimum maximum dot inner cross norm norm2 material region`, and conditions `lt gt le ge eq ne land lor lnot`. `abs(x)` is Python's, through `__abs__`. They accept symbolic values and plain numbers.
* **Where Monty stops us (1.6.0, measured).** A class's `__bool__`, `__lt__` and its siblings, `__ne__` and `__getattr__` are not called by Monty: `if sym:` takes the true branch, `not sym` is False, `sym > 0` is a `TypeError` of Monty's own, and `sym != 0` is the bool `True`. The plan's rule (a branch on a symbolic value is an error that says `where(...)`) cannot be kept by the runtime for these. What the runtime does keep: `==`, `float()`, `int()`, `round()`, `[..][sym]` and iterating raise our error that names `where(...)` (the dunders Monty does call).
* **A static guard keeps the rule.** Before a script runs (and in `nyx check`) `nyx_script::trace::guard` parses it (`ruff_python_parser`, the parser Monty uses, pinned the same) and finds the functions passed to a `nyx.` call (a name of a `def`, or a `lambda`, directly or in a list), with the functions they call by name. In them it follows which names depend on the point (the parameter, anything assigned from an expression that mentions one, loop and comprehension variables over one, the parameters of a helper called with one, including through containers) and refuses an `if`, `while`, `a if c else b`, `and`, `or`, `not`, a comprehension condition, `assert` or a comparison whose test mentions one, and `math.` calls on them, with the line, the text of the rule and the `where(...)` spelling to use. A branch on something that does not depend on the point (`if USE_CORRECTION:`, `for k in range(3)`) is allowed, as in JAX. Limit, stated in the contract: the guard is a syntactic over-approximation; a value hidden from it (a symbolic value stored in a structure the guard does not follow, a function chosen at run time) is not seen, and then `if sym:` takes the true branch. **Paul may prefer a Monty that dispatches `__bool__`** (an upstream change) over this guard; the guard then becomes a second line of defence.
* **Contract.** `script_api` 1.1 (additive): the traced-function form, the names, the guard. The stub gains the prelude's names so the static check knows them. The user's script is fed after the prelude as its own feed, with the prelude fed without the type check, so traceback line numbers are the user's.

## Not in this decision

* A code generator (N4).
* Convergence of an integral under refinement (a reduction reads one result on one mesh).
* Reductions in a worker process: they read the result the parent holds and take about as long as reading it.
* Maxima of the interpolant between nodes.

## Consequences

* `engine_commands` gains eight commands and `result_info` gains `cell_fields` (additive); `mcp_tools` gains eight tools (additive). Versions 1.15 and 2.10 (after the merge with main). N2 changes only descriptions (1.17 and 2.12). N2b adds arguments (`boundary`, `side`, `wavelength`, `weight`) and so is 1.18 and 2.13; nothing is removed.
* `Stored` holds the mesh model of its result, so a result keeps its mesh alive until it is replaced.
* `nyx check` treats the eight commands as readers of a result.
* N3 changes no engine command and no MCP tool: the engine receives the same formula text. It adds a Python prelude to every script run (a few milliseconds), the names `where`, `sqrt`, ... `trace`, `region`, `material` to a script's globals (a script may still use them as variable names; the stub declares them as `Any`), the `ruff_python_parser` crates (the parser Monty already links) to `nyx-script`, and `script_api` 1.1.

## Code

* `crates/femcore/src/fieldexpr.rs` (the tree and its evaluator), `crates/femcore/src/formula.rs` (the formula parser), `crates/nyx-engine/src/reduce.rs` (the commands and the names of a formula), `crates/nyx-engine/src/engine.rs` (`Stored.model`), `crates/app/src/tabs.rs` (the Reduce form). N2b: `Namer::component`, `Prep::boundary_faces`, `integrate_boundary` in `reduce.rs`; the formula box in `tabs.rs`.
* N3: `crates/nyx-script/src/trace.rs` (the prelude, the stub names, the guard) and `crates/nyx-script/src/prelude.nys` (the symbolic value, the point, the tracer); `host::drive` feeds the prelude and calls the guard. Tests: `crates/nyx-script/tests/trace.rs` (ten traced integrands equal their written formulas to the bit with the function called once, a traced `weight`, `probe`, `line_cut`, `nyx.call` and a positional dict, the text with its parentheses and operand order, the branch rule on fifteen refused and five allowed scripts, `nyx check`); sample `docs/scripting-samples/traced_formulas.nys`.
* Tests: `crates/nyx-engine/tests/reduce.rs` (the sapphire tensor, the wavelength, the energy fraction, line and surface integrals against closed forms and the divergence theorem, closed forms, loops to the bit, thread counts, a worker result, a real mode and a real thermal field), `crates/app/src/app.rs` (the form shows the engine's numbers).
decisions.title: Whole-array operations on results are engine commands over a typed expression tree evaluated in Rust

# 91. Validated is a state: a result is checked only by a convergence check on its own problem key

Date: 2026-11-18

## Status

Accepted as step P6 of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3). **Number 91: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.**

## Context

`convergence_check` (ADR 61) has been an engine command, an MCP tool and a Study-tab button for a long time, but its answer lived and died with the call. A result that had been checked and one that had not looked the same in `result_info`, in the window and in the run table, so a number could be quoted, or a run kept, without anything saying whether anyone had looked at the mesh. The plan asks for validation to be a state a reader can see, and adds a third state for the case the plan found in its own measurements: in 3D the check solves on a mesh finer by a factor, unknowns grow as `factor^-3` and the memory of a direct factorisation grows faster, so the check may be the one thing the machine cannot do, and a 3D result must not look merely "unchecked".

## Decision

* **Three states, one reason each** (`nyx_engine::validated`). `exploratory`: no convergence check with a stated tolerance has passed on this problem (this is also the state of a result whose last check failed, with the numbers of that check as the reason). `checked`: a check with a tolerance passed. `check_not_affordable`: not checked, and the check is expected not to fit this machine. Every answer that carries `stale` also carries `validated: {state, reason, check?}`: `project_info`, `result_info`, `result_field`, `analyse` and the reductions of ADR 90 (a reduction over several physics reports the weakest state, with one row per physics).
* **A verdict belongs to a problem, not to a result.** The engine keeps the checks it has seen by the problem key of ADR 84 (`Engine::problem_key`, taken when the check starts). A result is checked when a passed check exists for its own key. So a result solved again from the same problem, a file opened, or a project edited back to an earlier state is checked again, and an edited project is not: **a stale result is never checked**, whatever was checked before. The last check of a problem decides (a later failing check turns it back to `exploratory`).
* **A tolerance is what makes a verdict.** A check without `tolerance` records nothing and the state does not move. With one, `passed` means every compared quantity was within it, the rule `convergence_check` always had.
* **What was compared is said.** The verdict names its observable (every eigenvalue, value and numeric scalar of the result, the number of them) and how solutions were matched: **by index**, the order the solver returns them. Matching by overlap or tracking (plan R11) is not built; a 3D check over many near-degenerate modes can therefore pass or fail on a reordering, and the verdict says "matched by index" so nobody reads more into it.
* **Not affordable is an estimate, with its basis.** With no check, the engine takes the cells of the result, the cells of a mesh finer by the planned factor (0.6: `cells / 0.6^dim`) and asks the memory history of ADR 86 for that size (`History::estimate`); when the estimate with its margin exceeds the fraction of this machine's memory that admission refuses (`REFUSE_ABOVE`, 90 %), the state is `check_not_affordable` and the reason names the estimate, the runs it was fitted to and whether it is extrapolated. With no estimate nothing is claimed (the state is `exploratory`: the engine does not know that the check is out of reach). A check that was made always beats the estimate.
* **The run record keeps the verdict.** `nyx_store::runs::RunRecord` gains the optional `convergence: {factor, tolerance, observable, passed, worst_relative}`, written as a patch line (the same mechanism as star, tags and note: nothing is rewritten, the last patch wins), so a run table and a later session know the run was checked. The field is optional and written only when there is a verdict: every earlier `runs.jsonl` and the `store_run.v1` exemplar are unchanged and no format key moves (ADR 63 concerns project, feature list and problem-spec files, not run lines). The engine writes the patch into the run that solved the problem when it records runs (`Stored.run`); the window, which writes its own run records, writes it into the run on show (`App::note_check_in_run`).
* **The window** shows the state as a glyph and a word, never by colour alone (`kit::State`: `Checked` a ring with a check mark, `Exploratory` a ring half filled, `NotAffordable` a ring with a slash; ADR 88): a chip on the plot, and a line with the reason and a "Check convergence" button in the Results tab and under the convergence form of the Study tab. Nothing is drawn for a stale result: the stale band says it.

## Consequences

* An agent or a person can see whether a number rests on a check, and a failed check is as visible as a passed one. A script can refuse to quote an `exploratory` number.
* The check is still two solves, run through the queue like any heavy job (ADR 87); this decision adds no work to a solve.
* What the check compares decides what "checked" is worth: the 04 thermal bar's scalars are its boundary temperatures, so it passes any tolerance. `observable` is in the verdict for that reason; choosing the quantity a check must be about (a mode's effective index, a stress) is a later argument of `convergence_check`, not built here.
* A physics that takes fields from another is checked the way `convergence_check` solves it, on its own; its verdict is stored under its own problem key (which includes its imports' keys), so a change in the physics it imports makes it stale as before.

## Not in this decision

* Cheaper evidence counted as partial support: the Maxwell residual estimator (ADR 53), a two-mesh ladder, a Richardson estimate. None of them leaves a stored number on a result today; when one does, it belongs in `validated.check` as a second kind of evidence, not in a fourth state.
* Tracking modes between the two meshes (plan R11), a convergence check of a reduction (ADR 90) over refinement, a column for the verdict in the runs table, and a filter term for it.

## Code

`crates/nyx-engine/src/validated.rs`, `convergence.rs` (the answer names the worst quantity, the count and the matching), `engine.rs` (`checks`, `Stored.run`, `Pending::Convergence { physics, key }`), `crates/nyx-store/src/runs.rs` (`Convergence`, the patch), `crates/app/src/{activity,kit,shell,app}.rs`. Tests: `crates/nyx-engine/tests/validated.rs`, the store test of the patch, the window test `the_window_shows_the_validated_state_and_a_check_goes_into_the_run`.

## Contract

`engine_commands` 1.16 and `mcp_tools` 2.11 (additive: `validated` in the answers above, `recorded`, `run`, `worst_quantity`, `quantities` and `matching` in the `convergence_check` answer); `store_run` stays 1.0 (an optional key that is absent unless a check was made).
decisions.title: Validated is a state: a result is checked only by a convergence check on its own problem key

# 92. Feedback while editing is a value, never a job

Date: 2026-11-18

## Status

Accepted as step P3 of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3). **Number 92: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.**

## Context

The plan applies the paper's point (a response inside a second keeps the train of thought) **per interaction**, and says that nothing ever starts a mesh-and-solve chain on its own. P3 had to decide, interaction by interaction, from numbers measured on the merged build (UX stack and P6 included; `docs/PRODUCTIVITY_STATUS.md`, section "P3 done"), which ones need work and which are left alone. The measurements, on this machine (i5-13500), with a frame log that now says where each frame's time went (`NYX_FRAME_LOG` with `spans`):

* **Viewing** (rotate, switch solution or field, 3D cavity of 9,480 cells, 56,226 unknowns, a second solve running): frame p95 18.4 ms, p99 19.3 ms, max 25.8 ms. The data pass of 362 field and solution switches took 2.5 ms at most. The gate (33 ms) holds and nothing is precomputed.
* **Geometry preview, input check, mesh, on every example** (a fresh engine per repetition): geometry 0.05 to 0.51 ms, check 0.01 to 0.09 ms, first mesh build 0.5 to 12.1 ms (2D up to 8,012 cells; 3D swept up to 6,936 cells). Inside the 100 ms of the plan everywhere.
* **Run table at 500 runs:** UI 4.4 ms p50, 6.0 ms p95, frame p95 18 ms. Inside the budget, left alone.
* **Polarization** costs 1.4 to 5 microseconds per cell on the UI thread (9 ms at 9,480 cells in 3D, 15 ms at 10,800 cells of the SOI wire, 41 to 48 ms at the 8,012 cells of the silicon-on-sapphire example): over a frame at moderate sizes.
* **The frame in which a solve's result is taken** costs 53 to 63 ms (once per solve): the engine applying the result 9 to 19 ms, the polarization 9 ms, recording the run (files, digest, manifest) 9 to 18 ms, refreshing the dashboard entries 4 to 6 ms; the frame after it lays out the Results tab for the first time, 29 ms (13.8 ms of it the solver log, 20.7 ms the tab).

## Decision

* **Feedback is a value the front-end asks for, never a job.** Three engine functions answer a question about an edit that is not applied yet, or about a result, without changing the engine, its mesh, its results or its queue (`nyx_engine::preview`):
  * `check_edits(geometry, mesh)`: `Project::check` on a copy with the edits in place (the feature list, the element size, every problem against its physics). Microseconds; runs on every change of the Geometry form.
  * `size_preview(geometry, mesh)`: a `SizeTask`, `Send`, that meshes a copy of the edits (the mesher and sizing of the project, no stage cache) and looks up the memory and time estimate of ADR 86 for that many cells. The caller runs it on a thread of its own. Offered only where the mesh is cheap: 2D, and 3D swept from a 2D section; any other 3D mesh is refused with the reason ("can take seconds: it is built by Build mesh"). The answer says the cells, the dimension, the seconds the trial took and the estimate with its basis, or no estimate when fewer than two runs of different sizes exist (nothing is invented).
  * `polarization_task(physics)`: the analysis of ADR 56 as a function that owns its inputs, with the result it was made for, so a front-end can compute it beside the frame and tell whether the answer still belongs to what is on show.
* **The window** (`feedback.rs`) shows the problem of the edits as a glyph, the word "Problem" and the engine's words, and, if there is none, "About N cells, 2D (a trial mesh of these settings, not built)" with the cost line, under the mesh controls of the Geometry form. The trial mesh starts when an edit has rested for 200 ms and is dropped if the edit moved on. **A trial mesh that takes 100 ms or more turns the automatic preview off** (the rule of plan question 2), says so, and waits for the person ("Estimate size"). The polarization of a new result is computed on a thread and lands in the result view that holds that very result.
* **The mesh preview is numbers, not a drawing.** The plan allowed a small 2D mesh preview if P0 showed the mesher cheap; it is cheap (at most 12 ms), and what the person needs while editing the element size is the count and the cost. Drawing a trial mesh in the viewport needs a viewport content that is not the engine's model, which the UX stack owns; it is not built, and a later decision can add it on top of `size_preview` (the task already meshes the edits).
* **No mesh, solve, run or job without a request** is a test, not a promise: `editing_every_form_starts_nothing` edits every buffered form of the window (element size, sizing from the physics, adaptive, absorbing layers, sweep of the mesh, a refused size, and the Sweep form of the Build page), draws frames until every check and trial mesh has run (and asserts the last one came back), and asserts that no job was submitted, no run recorded, the engine's mesh and project are the same objects, the result on show is still there and nothing is busy. Compute, a queue submission, Run sweep and an MCP command remain the only things that start work.
* **Left alone, with the numbers above:** viewing, the geometry preview of the feature list, the run table, solving (a request), convergence checks, exports and sweeps (background requests). Not changed in this step although they are over a frame once per solve: recording the run, applying the result in the engine and the first layout of the Results tab. Each is named, with its cost, in the status file as follow-up work.
* **Diagnostics:** `NYX_FRAME_LOG` rows gain a `spans` column (`spans.rs`: named timings of `poll`, `take_solved`, `record_ok`, the Results tab and its parts). Nothing is read or stored when the variable is unset. The example `p3measure` times the check, the cold mesh and the polarization on every example project.

## Consequences

* An edit that cannot be built is named at once, not at Compute; the size of an edit is on screen before a mesh is built; the polarization no longer lengthens the frame in which a result arrives (by 9 ms at 9,480 cells, more on finer 2D meshes).
* A trial mesh is a second mesh of the same edits when Build mesh is pressed. That costs milliseconds for the models it is offered for and nothing for the others; the stage cache of the engine is deliberately not used for it, so a trial mesh can never become the mesh a solve reads.
* The estimate is only as good as the runs this machine has done; the line says "no cost estimate yet" until two sizes exist.
* An analysis computed on a thread can arrive after the person has moved on: it is applied only to the result view that holds the very result it was computed from (`Arc::ptr_eq`), otherwise dropped.

## Code

`crates/nyx-engine/src/preview.rs`, `analyse.rs` (`analysis_inputs` is crate-visible), `engine.rs` (`store_results`), `estimate.rs` (the history writer), `crates/nyx-store/src/flow.rs` (one manifest write per run), `crates/app/src/{feedback,spans,app,tabs,script,shell,wfview}.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/examples/p3measure.rs`, `tools/ux-shots.sh` (two more shots). Tests: `crates/nyx-engine/tests/preview.rs` and the window tests `editing_every_form_starts_nothing`, `the_size_of_an_edit_arrives_from_a_trial_mesh` and `the_polarization_arrives_after_the_result_and_only_for_the_result_it_was_made_from`.

## Contract

None changed: no command was added and no answer changed, so `engine_commands`, `mcp_tools` and the exemplars keep their versions.

## Addendum: the frame that takes a result (same step, second commit)

The first commit left one stutter per solve: the frame that takes a result was 53 to 63 ms and the next one, which draws the Results tab for the first time, 37 to 45 ms. A frame log with spans attributed them, and each part was dealt with by what it is:

* **The engine's apply step copied every result** (`Arc::new(r.clone())`, 6 ms for 56,226 unknowns). Results are now moved into the store after the run is recorded (`Engine::store_results`); what is stored, and under which key, is unchanged. The failed-chain path stores what was solved as before.
* **The history appended to its file on the calling thread** (10 ms for an open and a write on this machine). `History::add` updates the rows in memory at once, which is what estimates read, and a thread of the history writes the line; lines are written in order, `flush` waits for them, and dropping the history flushes. The format of the file is unchanged.
* **The run record is 9 to 17 ms of file operations** (freeze the spec, read the run table twice, append, write the digest and the manifest). The store now writes the manifest once instead of twice per run, and the window writes the record **on the frame after the result is taken**, and the dashboard refresh (4 to 6 ms) on the one after that (`shell::Deferred`, one piece per `poll`, never in the frame that took a result). A solve's run context is taken with its result, so a second solve cannot be recorded under the first one's. Scripts and the test helper wait for the queue to be empty before going on.
* **The solver log starts closed.** Drawing its eleven short monospace lines for the first time cost 13 to 14 ms (one label for the whole log, and laying the glyphs out beforehand, both measured the same or worse and were dropped); the header still says how many lines it holds. This is a visible default changed on purpose, and `default_open` is the one place to change it back.

Measured again with the same 3D case, every frame around a result is now at most 31 ms (the worst: the first Results draw 30.6 ms, the run record 28.8 ms), against 53 to 63 and 37 to 45 ms.
decisions.title: Feedback while editing is a value, never a job

# 93. Scripts are Python-syntax text run by Monty in a worker process, behind an engine path guard

Date: 2026-11-18

## Status

**Amended by ADR 94** (provisional number, productivity plan S7): the MCP server offers four script tools, `script_run`, `script_wait`, `script_check` and `api`, instead of one tool per engine command, after Paul's answer to Q9 (2026-11-19); the engine commands themselves are unchanged.

Accepted as step S4 of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3b), after Paul's choice (2026-11-18). **Number 93: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.** Amends ADR 57 (the front-ends over `Engine::call` are now three: the window, the MCP server, scripts) and uses ADR 86 (work that can take the process down runs in a child process). Python stays out in the sense of ADR 13: no CPython is embedded or needed; Monty is a Python-syntax interpreter written in Rust, and Paul accepted it on that reading.

## Context

An agent or a person who wants a workflow with loops, decisions and sweeps had two choices: one tool call per command (ADR 15, the cost S1 to S3 reduced), or a JSON command list (ADR 89), which has no loops and no decisions. The plan wanted a third thin front-end: a text file in an embedded, pure-Rust language that calls engine commands. The S4 spike bound three candidates to the whole catalog and ran the same sample in each (`docs/PRODUCTIVITY_STATUS.md`, S4 spike). The numbers were the same in all three, and the interpreter's cost (1 to 25 microseconds per call) is not a factor against solves of seconds. What differed:

* **Starlark** turns on `serde_json`'s `arbitrary_precision` for every crate of the build, which breaks nine tests (three untagged enums, one of them part of the file format); it cannot loop with `while`, has no `try`, no `%.2f`, and a Python writer's first top-level `for` is an error.
* **Rhai** is clean to build and bounds memory in-process, but its syntax is new to every reader and every model.
* **Monty** takes real Python syntax (nothing to unlearn; an agent writes it natively), has no side effect on the build, and gives CPython-style errors with the line. It needs a process boundary for memory: a script that doubles a list in a loop aborts the process the interpreter runs in.

Two gates of the plan were not met by any candidate in the spike: a script must not read or write a file outside the workspace, and a script that allocates without bound must be stopped.

## Decision

* **Language: Monty 1.6.0** (crates `monty-pool`, `monty-types`, `monty-proto`, `monty-alloc`, MIT, pinned with `=`). A script is a text file `*.nys` (the extension is ours: `*.py` is git-ignored in this repository on purpose, CLAUDE.md). Its value is its last expression; what it prints and returns is all that goes back. Engine commands are `nyx.<command>(name=value, ...)`, one method per entry of `Engine::catalog()` (nothing is listed by hand, ADR 57), plus `nyx.call(name, **args)`; an engine error is raised as `RuntimeError("<command>: <message>")`, which the script can catch.
* **The interpreter runs in a worker process, never in the engine's** (`nyx-script-worker`, a program of the `nyx-script` package: Monty's own worker mode, vendored as one 100-line file so that building nyx builds its worker and nothing is installed beside it). The engine stays in the host process: each command a script makes pauses the script, the host answers with `Engine::call`, and the script goes on (Monty's native model). A script that allocates without bound, overflows the stack or hangs ends one worker and the host goes on (`tests/script.rs`: doubling a list and a string, `[0] * 10**12`, `while True`). One worker per run, none kept.
* **Limits are strict by default and raised per run** (`Limits`): 30 s of script time (**the time the host spends answering a command is not counted**, so a 40 s solve is not script time), 256 MiB for the worker, call depth 100, 20,000 commands, 1 MiB of output. `nyx run FILE.nys --seconds N --memory MB --calls N` raises them. The pool also kills a worker that is silent past the time limit plus ten seconds.
* **No ambient access** (ADR 11, 13). The sandbox has no file, network, environment or process access; `open`, `pathlib` and `os` raise `PermissionError` with the path. **The clock is refused** (`RuntimeError`), **`random` starts from the fixed seed 0** (CPython's `random.seed(0)` sequence), `sleep` returns at once: the same script and inputs give the same numbers.
* **The path guard is in the engine** (`nyx_engine::path_guard`, `Engine::set_path_root`), not in the script host: with a root set, every argument named `path`, `folder` or `workspace` of any command is rewritten to an absolute path inside the root (a relative path is taken from the root) or the command fails before it runs; `..`, an absolute path elsewhere, a sibling folder with the same prefix and a link or junction out of the root are refused. `PATH_ARGS` names the guarded arguments and a test over the catalog fails when a command takes a path-like argument not in it (it found `store_save.workspace` while this was written). The host turns the guard on for a run, with the script's workspace (else the script's folder) as root, and restores it after.
* **A static check runs before every script and as `nyx check FILE.nys`.** Monty type-checks the script against a stub generated from the catalog (`nyx_script::stubs::nyx_pyi`, also `nyx api stubs`): a misspelled command or argument, a missing required argument, an unknown module and a syntax error fail in milliseconds with the line named and nothing ran. **Names and required-ness are checked, not value types**: the catalog says `number` for a field that also takes an expression text (`"w/2"`), and a check that refuses what the engine accepts is worse than none. The same stub, saved as `nyx.pyi` next to a script, gives an editor the commands and their documentation.
* **A run keeps the script that made it**: while a script runs the engine holds its text, and each run it records (`solve_run`, a sweep point) gets the file `script-<hash>.nys` in its folder (blake3, 32 hex digits, as the store hashes everything) with an artifact of kind `script`. No field of the run record changes, so no file format and no exemplar moves.
* **`nyx check FILE.nys` and `nyx run FILE.nys`** extend S1's commands to scripts (a file ending in `.nys`); `run` checks first.

## Consequences

* The worker is a second program to ship: `nyx-script-worker` next to `nyx` (35 MB, most of it the bundled type checker). The program finds it in its own folder or in `NYX_SCRIPT_WORKER`; without it a script fails with that sentence.
* Building the workspace now also builds Monty and its type checker (`ty`), about two minutes cold. `Cargo.lock` pins `salsa` to 0.28.2, the version Monty's own lock file pins (0.28.5, which cargo picks otherwise, does not compile with `ruff_python_ast` 0.0.14). The `monty-*` crates must move together.
* Monty is nine months old; its Python subset is large but not complete (no third-party modules, `assert` messages are pytest-style, a script that ends in an assignment returns nothing). Errors say what is missing (`ModuleNotFoundError`, a type-check message). Its sandbox is young: the path guard and the worker's isolation are ours and are tested here, and the interpreter's own isolation is relied on, not audited.
* A script's start-up costs a process: about 0.14 s measured (spawn and type check; 0.85 s the first time after a build, while the 35 MB worker is read from disk). A script is for a workflow, not for a loop of cheap commands; per-element work is a missing engine command (ADR 90).

## Not in this decision

* **A plan (dry run) of a script.** A script's commands depend on its results (a convergence loop, `if res["stale"]`), so a dry run that answers commands with placeholders cannot follow it. `nyx check FILE.nys` is the static stage only. What the script would mesh and solve can be shown from a run (the queue's estimates, ADR 86), not before it. A way to plan a script is an open design point.
* Submitting a script to the queue as one request with an owner (plan Q3), the MCP script mode (S7), a script browser in the dashboard (`scripts/` is a folder convention: the workspace's scripts live there, nothing lists them yet), N2 formulas and N3 tracing of script functions (S5, S6).
* A pool of kept workers: one worker per run costs about 0.14 s and is the simplest thing that isolates.

## Code

`crates/nyx-script/src/{lib,host,convert,stubs}.rs`, `crates/nyx-script/src/bin/nyx-script-worker.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/src/path_guard.rs` (and `Engine::{set_path_root, set_script}`, `commands.rs` `call`, `store_link.rs`, `sweep.rs`), `crates/app/src/{runfile,apicmd}.rs`. Tests: `crates/nyx-script/tests/script.rs`, `crates/nyx-script/tests/contract.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/tests/path_guard.rs` and the unit tests of `path_guard.rs`. Samples: `docs/scripting-samples/strip_sweep.nys`.

## Contract

`script_api.v1` (`docs/architecture/contracts/script_api.v1.json`): what a script can rely on: the extension, the object and its call forms, the default limits, the guarded argument names, the clock and random policy, the script artifact. The commands themselves are `engine_commands`.
decisions.title: Scripts are Python-syntax text run by Monty in a worker process, behind an engine path guard

# 94. The MCP server is four script tools over one long-lived kernel

Date: 2026-11-19

## Status

Accepted as step S7 of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3b), after Paul's answer to Q9 on 2026-11-19: **script tools only; the one-tool-per-command catalog is deleted, not kept behind a flag.** **Number 94: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.** Amends ADR 15 (the MCP tool list), ADR 57 (the MCP server's tools are no longer the catalog) and ADR 93 (the script host becomes a kernel that outlives one script).

## Context

ADR 57 made every engine command an MCP tool: 99 tools, about 50 KB of definitions, one call per command, and every result sent twice (as text and as `structuredContent`). S1 to S3 cut the calls an agent needs, S4 gave scripts, S5 and S6 gave them formulas. An agent that has to make five calls to change one width, resend a whole model description to do it, and read the full project JSON to find one feature is paying for the interface and not for the physics. Anthropic's "Code execution with MCP" and Cloudflare's "Code Mode" make the same point: the agent writes code against a typed API and only what the code prints comes back.

Monty (ADR 93) is more than "a script runs". Measured on 1.6.0 with a stand-in host (2026-11-19):

* **A paused script is a coroutine the host steps.** It stays paused at a host call for as long as the host likes: a 20 s gap passed with a 5 s feed limit and a 15 s request timeout. Host time is not script time.
* **State persists between feeds.** Variables and functions of one feed are known to the next, and the static check knows them too: `x = 41` then `x + 1` passes, a misspelled name or argument in a later feed is still refused with its line. An input (`params`) declared in the stub type-checks.
* **A session can be dumped and restored**: 1.4 KB idle, 2.5 KB paused at a host call, restored in a new worker with variables, functions and the host module binding intact. The dump holds the interpreter only, not the engine.
* **Futures work.** A host answers a call to an async function with `ResumeValue::Future` and settles it on `TurnEvent::ResolveFutures`; top-level `await`, `asyncio.gather` (also over a list comprehension, and from an `async def` of the script), start now and await later, and an exception raised at the `await` all work. `gather(return_exceptions=True)` and `asyncio.create_task` do not exist in 1.6.0. Three 0.5 s timer jobs gathered took 0.51 s against 1.53 s awaited one by one. **That gain is not carried over to solves**: the engine's heavy lane runs one solve at a time (ADR 87), so futures give pipelining (post-process each point as it finishes) and overlap with light work, not faster heavy solves.
* Monty has no screenshots.

## Decision

* **Four tools, and no others.**
  * `script_run {source | path, params, wait_s, allow_destructive, save_as}`: runs a script and answers `done`, `running` or `error`.
  * `script_wait {wait_s, cancel}`: continues a script that answered `running`, or abandons it.
  * `script_check {source | path}`: the static check of ADR 93 (parse, type-check against the stub, the traced-function guard of ADR 90 N3), nothing runs.
  * `api {topic | command}`: the API text. Without arguments: the instructions and the list of commands with their titles. A guide card (`geometry`, `optical-modes`, `troubleshooting`) or one command with its full description and arguments.
  The 99 per-command tools, `get_guide` as a tool, `nyx-mcp --list` and `--call`, the per-tool annotations and the per-result header are removed. The engine commands stay: the window and the scripts use them (`engine_commands` is unchanged). `--job` stays: it is the engine's solve worker (ADR 86).
* **One kernel.** The server creates a kernel on the first script call (so `initialize` and `tools/list` need no worker): one runtime, one worker pool, one Monty session that lives until the server stops. Variables, functions and imports of one `script_run` are there in the next. One script runs at a time; `script_run` while another is `running` is an error that names it.
* **A call never blocks for ever.** `solve_run`, `convergence_check`, `job_wait` and `queue_wait` are served by the host as: start the job without waiting, then poll `job_wait` with `timeout_s` 0 until it finished, the call's own timeout passed (`job_wait`, `queue_wait`), or the time given by `wait_s` (default 25 s) is spent. In the last case the script stays paused at the call and `script_run` answers `running` with what the script printed so far; `script_wait` continues the same poll. The value the script gets is the value the blocking call would have given. A job that cannot start (the engine says why) is an error, not an endless `running`. The host's own polling is not a script command: it does not count against `Limits.calls` and is not in the run record.
* **`params`.** A dict given to `script_run` is the script's input named `params` (declared in the stub, so it type-checks); a hand-written script reads `params.get("w", 500e-9)`. A saved script is run again with other values and nothing is resent.
* **Saved scripts** are `<workspace>/scripts/<name>.nys`. `path` is the name (letters, digits, `_ - .`, no folder); `save_as` stores the script just run. Nothing else in the file system is reachable (ADR 93's guard is unchanged).
* **Destructive commands need a flag.** `project_new`, `project_load`, `project_open`, `store_open` and every `remove_*` raise `RuntimeError` in a script unless `script_run` was called with `allow_destructive: true`, which the host's approval dialog shows with the call. The list lives in `nyx-script` (the MCP server used to carry it). `nyx run` allows them: a person runs their own file.
* **Results are text, once.** One JSON object: `status`, `value`, `printed` (capped at `Limits.output_bytes`), `calls`, the script's hash and the project header `nyx {session, revision, project_hash}` once per answer instead of once per command. No `structuredContent`.
* **A crashed worker costs the call, not the session.** After every finished script the host keeps an in-memory dump; when the worker dies (memory limit, stack) the next call restores the last dump into a new worker, so variables survive. Dumps are not written to disk: a restart of the server starts a new kernel (the interpreter state is not the engine's, and a dump is not authenticated).
* **`script_run`, `nyx run` and `nyx check` share one driver** (`nyx_script::kernel`); `host::run` and `host::check` are thin wrappers over it.
* **Futures (`nyx.aio`).** Decided after the poll loop above exists: the async twins `await nyx.aio.solve_run(...)`, `nyx.aio.convergence_check`, `nyx.aio.job_wait` reuse it. A future left pending when a feed ends, aborts or fails has its engine job cancelled.

## Consequences

* An agent works in one to three calls where it made five to forty, and fields and tables stay in the engine; only what the script prints comes back.
* The `mcp_tools` contract is a major version: four tools. The 50 KB `mcp_tools.v2.json` snapshot is replaced; the full catalog remains pinned by `engine_commands`, which is what the window and scripts use. `script_api` gains `params` and the kernel semantics (additive).
* `nyx-mcp` depends on `nyx-script` (layering table), and `nyx-script-worker` must sit next to `nyx-mcp` (`NYX_SCRIPT_WORKER`). `cargo test -p nyx-mcp` alone does not build the worker; the tests that run a script say so.
* **Known limits.** The traced-function guard (ADR 90 N3) reads the source of one feed: a function defined in an earlier `script_run` and passed as a formula in a later one is not seen by it. The dump does not hold the engine: a restarted server has to reopen the project. The window and the server are separate processes with their own engines (ADR 57): a project the agent saves is reopened in the window, there is no live link. `gather(return_exceptions=True)` and `create_task` are missing in Monty 1.6.0.
* Not built: scripts saved by the window ("export this model as a script"), a plan (dry run) mode, dumps on disk.

## Export as script (S7b)

A person who builds a model in the window, with no script, can hand it to an agent as a script: **File > Export as script...** writes `.nys` text that rebuilds the project, and the engine command `project_script` (read-only, so `nyx.project_script()` in a script and an MCP agent have it too) returns the same text. The agent then runs it with `script_run` and changes a value with `params`, and the person's model is the starting point of a script and not a JSON blob.

* **The commands, then the text.** The engine builds a list of `(command, arguments)` and renders it as Python; it does not format text first. The list is, in this order: `project_new(dim, title)`; `set_param` per parameter in stored order, written `value=params.get("w", 5e-07)`, so `script_run path=... params={"w": 3e-7}` is the variant with nothing edited; `add_<kind>(name=..., <args>)` per feature (`geometry::describe` gives the arguments in the form the add command takes), then `suppress_feature` and `tag_feature`; `set_mesh` with the fields that differ from the default; `add_material` per project material; `set_problem` per physics with the problem as a dict; `set_active`.
* **Verified before it is offered.** The list is replayed on a scratch engine and the result must equal the project. Equal means the project JSON with every feature's `origin` set to `Code` on both sides (the window's features are `Gui`, `add_*` makes `Code`; origin changes no result), and, when no overlay has pins or pinned regions, with the feature ids renumbered (a window model whose features were removed has id gaps; replay renumbers them). Three forms, first that verifies: `commands` (the list above); `geometry_json` (the same, with the geometry as one `set_geometry`: exact ids, for models whose pins refer to them); `project_json` (one `project_load` of the whole project: always exact, not readable). The answer says which, and so does the header comment of the script. The tests require `commands` for every example project, so a fallback cannot hide a bug.
* **Rendering.** `true`, `false` and `null` become `True`, `False` and `None`; numbers keep the shortest text that reads back to the same value; strings are written as JSON strings (valid Python); a dict or list longer than a line is laid out over lines. The text holds no file path, so it does not depend on the path guard's root, and it starts with `project_new`: over MCP it needs `script_run allow_destructive: true`, which the header comment says.
* **The window** pushes its buffered edits first (as Save does), asks the engine, and writes the file (default folder the MCP server's `scripts` folder, `Documents/nyx_runs/mcp/scripts`, so an agent runs it with `script_run path=<name>`; `nyx_script::mcp_dir` is the one place that path is made). Contract: `engine_commands` 1.19 (additive: `project_script`).
* **Not exported:** results, meshes and the run history (they are outputs), the window's view settings and the title bar state. A script never solves; the person or the agent adds `nyx.solve_run()`.

## Code

`nyx-script::{kernel,host,stubs,prelude}`, `nyx-mcp::main`, `nyx-engine::{guide,cards,scriptout}`, `app::app` (File menu); contracts `mcp_tools` 3.0, `script_api` 1.2, `engine_commands` 1.19.
decisions.title: The MCP server is four script tools over one long-lived kernel
