# 95. The queue is a folder of the workspace, run by a queue worker that outlives the window

Date: 2026-11-19

## Status

Accepted as step Q3 of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3a), with Paul's "yes" of 2026-11-19. **Number 95: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.** Builds on ADR 86 (solves in worker processes, memory admission) and ADR 87 (lanes, priorities, owners); amends ADR 57 (the front-ends share one queue, not only the commands) and ADR 86 (the queue worker is a second kind of worker).

## Context

ADR 87 gave each `Engine` a queue; ADR 86 put every solve in a child process. The window and the MCP server are still two programs with an engine each, so a person's Compute and an agent's solve run side by side on one machine, with their memory added up, and closing the window ends what it was waiting for. Plan Q3 asks for one queue that every front-end reads and steers, that survives a front-end, and that survives the death of a worker, with no daemon to install and no network.

## Decision

* **The queue is the folder `queue/` of a workspace.** An item is a folder `queue/items/<id>/` that a front-end writes whole (a temporary folder renamed into place): `request.json` (owner, priority, label, targets, the hash of the frozen project, the memory estimate the front-end made), `project.nyx.json` and `job.json` (exactly what a worker of ADR 86 is given). The id sorts by submission time. A front-end writes nothing else but **markers**: an empty file `cancel`, an empty file `hold` (removed to release), a file `priority`. **No file has two writers**: the queue worker alone writes `state.json` (an item with none is queued), `order.json` (the ids in the order they will start, which is what a front-end shows as the place in the queue), the results (`results.h5`, `stderr.txt`) and the lease.
* **The queue worker is `PROGRAM --worker WORKSPACE`**, a process of its own (`nyx`, `nyx-mcp` and `nyx-worker` all answer it). It takes the lease, ranks the items with the job runner's rules (priority, lowered one level for each minute waited, then the owners in turns, then submission order), runs the head in a solver child exactly as ADR 86 does (`worker::run_child`, the one place a worker is started; `tests/worker.rs`'s bit comparison covers it), admits it by memory (ADR 86's `admit`, here and nowhere else, so nothing is admitted twice), appends the run to `solve_history.jsonl` (so the estimates are learned whoever was watching), and ends after 30 s with nothing to do (`NYX_QUEUE_IDLE_SECS`). It does **not** end with the program that started it, unlike a job's worker: it is started detached (no console, no standard input, outside the job object of the starter), so closing the window or the terminal leaves it running. The solver children it starts keep ADR 86's rule: they end with it.
* **The lease** is `queue/runner.lock`, taken with `create_new` and kept alive by touching its modification time every second; one not touched for six seconds is dead. A process id alone is not trusted (Windows reuses them). Two programs that find a dead lease both try; one `create_new` wins and each reads the file back to see whose token is in it. A queue worker that finds the previous one's item `running` marks it `failed: the queue worker that was running this item stopped` (its solver child went with it).
* **A front-end that waits is a job in the new `shared` lane.** `solve_run`, `queue_submit` and `sweep_run` take `shared` (the window and the MCP server set it as the default with `Engine::set_shared_queue(folder, true)`; a solve that cannot be isolated runs in the process as before). The job meshes (one mesh at a time across such jobs, so fifty sweep points do not start fifty meshers), writes the item, makes sure a queue worker runs (and starts another if the lease goes stale while it waits), shows the item's place and then the queue worker's stage as its own progress, turns a cancel of the job into the `cancel` marker, reads the results file as it does a worker's, and removes the item. The lane has no limit that matters, so a job that is only queued remotely holds no core and no memory of the process and blocks neither the engine's heavy lane nor a convergence check. A cancel of a running item kills its solver at once (the queue worker polls the marker every 100 ms).
* **`queue_list` shows the whole queue**: the engine's own jobs and the items other programs wrote, marked `foreign`, each with a `shared_id`. `queue_get`, `queue_cancel`, `queue_hold`, `queue_release` and `queue_set_priority` take `shared_id` instead of `id` for those; `queue_pause` and `queue_resume` also write the queue's `pause` marker. `queue_submit {detached: true}` writes an item and returns at once with nothing waiting for it; the answer names `results`, the file `open_results` reads once the item is `done`.
* **The command line** is `nyx queue submit|list|cancel|hold|release|priority|pause|resume|clear WORKSPACE ...` (also `nyx-worker queue ...`).
* **Which folder.** The window uses its workspace (`NYX_WORKSPACE`, else `Documents/nyx`); the MCP server uses `--dir` when given, and otherwise the window's workspace (its own default, `Documents/nyx_runs/mcp`, keeps the scripts and nothing else of the queue). The cost history is the queue folder's file for any engine that has one set.
* **Ordering never changes a number** (ADR 11): an item is a frozen project; nothing carries from one item to the next, which is also the rule that confines the warm starts of the sweep plan (P5b) to one sweep request.

## Not in this decision

* **No run record for an item that finishes while nothing watches it.** The results wait in the item (`results.h5`, removed after 24 hours if nobody collects them); `open_results` reads them. A front-end that is open records the run as before.
* **Convergence checks, mesh builds and `open_results` stay in the process** and are not coordinated across programs; two programs can still run one of these each beside the queue worker's solve.
* **A hold, a priority change or a hold-at-submit for a job that is still meshing** (before its item exists) is refused; `hold: true` at submit works.
* **The order of the meshing stage between jobs of one engine is first come, not by priority** (the gate is a lock).
* **Position in the queue** is the queue worker's ranking at its last look (a quarter of a second old).
* **No backfill** (one heavy item at a time, as in ADR 86), no permissions per owner, no Q4 (workers on other machines).

## Consequences

* Closing the window leaves its queued and running items to the queue worker; reopening it lists them.
* A window and an MCP server on one workspace run one solve at a time, in order, instead of two at once.
* A queue worker process may remain for up to 30 s after the last item; it holds the workspace folder open, so deleting a workspace right after a run can fail once.
* `engine_commands` gains arguments and answer fields (additive, provisional 1.17); `mcp_tools` is unchanged (the four tools reach the commands through the script).

## Code

`crates/nyx-engine/src/{shared_queue,worker,queue,engine,jobs,estimate,commands}.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/src/bin/nyx-worker.rs`, `crates/app/src/{main,app}.rs`, `crates/nyx-mcp/src/main.rs`; tests `crates/nyx-engine/tests/shared_queue.rs`.

# 96. A sweep may start each point from the modes of the one before

Date: 2026-11-19

## Status

Accepted as step P5b of the productivity plan (`docs/NYX2_PRODUCTIVITY_PLAN.md`, section 3, "Reuse between solves"), with Paul's "yes build p5b" of 2026-11-19 after the measurement in `docs/PRODUCTIVITY_STATUS.md`. **Number 96: settled at the merge of the productivity line with main (2026-11-19), the next free number after the capability line.** Builds on ADR 87 and ADR 95 (the queue never lets one item change another's numbers) and ADR 91 (validated is a state).

## Context

A sweep that keeps its mesh solves the same eigenproblem many times with a small change. Each solve starts its shift-and-invert eigensolver from a pseudo-random block, and the iterations that follow take most of the time that is not the factorisation. Measured with a throw-away probe (status file, "P5b measured"): the previous point's wanted modes as the start block cut the eigensolve by about 40 % where the modes move, and a solve by **12 % to 20 %**; a sweep that changes the mesh (a width, a wavelength that sizes the mesh) has no start block to reuse and gains nothing. Plan P5a (bit-identical reuse of the symbolic factorisation) was measured at 1 to 14 % and skipped.

## Decision

* **Opt-in: `sweep_run {reuse: "warm"}`.** Without it nothing changes, bit for bit: no context is installed and the eigensolvers take the path they always took (`tests/worker.rs`, the goldens and `sweep.rs` run unchanged). There is no warm start outside a sweep; a request that is not a point of a warm sweep has no link, so **nothing ever carries between queue items** (ADR 95's rule).
* **The numerical core** (`femcore::warm`): a `Warm` context installed on the solving thread, like `progress`. The two shift-and-invert eigensolvers (`driver::eigs_near`, the Krylov-Schur path of the 3D cavity and the complex pencils, and `arnoldi_real::eigs_general`, the 2D mode solver) ask for a `Ticket`; the i-th eigensolve of a solve takes the i-th entry left by the previous solve if it is the same kind of solve on the same number of unknowns for the same number of modes, and starts cold otherwise (never an error: a start block can make a solve faster or slower, not wrong). `krylov_schur` takes a start of several columns (`given.min(block)`; one column, or none, is the block it always had). **All `nev` columns are warm**: replacing even one with a random column put the run back to cold speed in the measurement.
* **The chain.** Point i's link names the cell of point i-1 and the job that solves it. A point **waits** for its predecessor only in the `shared` lane (ADR 95), where it holds no core; in the heavy lane the lane runs points in order, so an unfinished predecessor is one that cannot finish (held, cancelled): the point is cold and says why (waiting would hold the lane for ever; tested). A point's cell is filled when its job ends, however it ends (`CellGuard`), so a point never waits for one that failed or never ran. Only a point that finished its whole chain hands its modes on. A warm sweep through the shared queue submits one point at a time (each waits for the one before), so the queue shows one point of it at a time.
* **The vectors travel as bytes** (`femcore::warm::to_bytes`): to a worker process in the job folder (`warm_in.bin` in, `warm_out.bin` and `warm_calls.json` out), and so also to the queue worker, whose item folder is a job folder. The three ways a solve runs give one answer (tested: the numbers are equal to the bit between in-process and worker, and equal through the queue worker).
* **The record.** A point's row and its run record (`reuse`, optional in `nyx_store::RunRecord`) say: `warm`, `from_point`, the restarts or cycles of every eigensolve, and for a warm point `exploratory: true` with the note that it agrees with a cold solve to the solver's tolerance, not bit for bit. A point that started cold says `why_cold` (the first point, a predecessor that had not finished, one that left no modes, nothing of the same size to start from).
* **A warm solve is never a cached coarse solve.** The engine does not keep a warm point's summary in the stage cache, so a mesh convergence check of the same problem solves its coarse mesh cold.

## Not in this decision (stated)

* **A warm result is not marked `exploratory` when it is opened from its run** (`open_results`): the results file does not carry `reuse`; the run record and the table row do. `validated` of ADR 91 applies to the engine's own results, which a sweep never replaces.
* **A start block of the old modes can miss a mode that enters the wanted window and is orthogonal to them.** In the measurement rounding noise let every entering mode be found (in as many restarts as a cold solve), but it is not guaranteed; that is why a warm point is not confirmed until solved cold. No second random block is added (it gave back the whole gain in the measurement).
* **Only the shift-and-invert eigensolvers are covered**: not LOBPCG, the direct solves of the static and transient studies, or the cavity solvers that do not use `eigs_near`. The factorisation is not reused (a new matrix at every point).
* **The window's sweep section sweeps geometry parameters, which change the mesh**, so it has no warm option; the command, scripts and the MCP server have.
* **Parallel warm points are not possible** (each needs the one before); a warm sweep is a chain.
* **No mode tracking** (R11) and no shifts taken from the previous eigenvalues: the shift stays what the study says, so a point's result does not depend on where it started except through the iteration.

## Consequences

* A warm sweep of a case that keeps its mesh solves 12 % to 20 % faster per point after the first; one that does not keep its mesh runs as a cold sweep and says why in every row.
* `engine_commands` gains the `reuse` argument of `sweep_run` and a `reuse` object in the rows of its table (additive, provisional 1.18). The run record gains an optional `reuse`.

## Code

`crates/femcore/src/{warm,linalg/driver,linalg/arnoldi_real,linalg/eps/krylov_schur}.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/src/{reuse,engine,sweep,worker,queue,store_link,commands}.rs`, `crates/nyx-store/src/runs.rs`; tests `crates/femcore/tests/warm.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/tests/warm_sweep.rs`.
decisions.title: A sweep may start each point from the modes of the one before

# 97. The MCP server reads while it waits, and says what a job costs

Date: 2026-11-20

## Status

Accepted as the latency work L1 to L3 (Paul, 2026-11-20: "do cap and the reader; yes fix the convergences; yes estimated times in all of them are useful; check the wildcard issue"). Amends ADR 94 (the waits of `script_run` and `script_wait`) and ADR 91 (what a convergence check counts). The number was free after ADR 96.

## Context

A benchmark session on 2026-11-19 (two silicon-on-sapphire waveguides driven from Antigravity through `nyx-mcp`) needed 3.8 s and 4.2 s of solving for the numbers it reported and took 35 and 13 minutes. What nyx contributed:

1. `script_run` accepted `wait_s` up to 900 and the server handled one line of stdin at a time. The host ends a call after 180 s; the server was still inside its 600 s wait, so the three calls the agent sent next queued behind it and each timed out after 180 s: 12 minutes.
2. `convergence_check` compares every number by its relative difference. A lossless guide on a tilted crystal runs the complex solver and has an imaginary part of 1e-10 that changes by 100 % between two meshes, and a quality factor of 1e10 made of it: `converged` stayed false and the agent went back to its planner twice.
3. A mesh of 22 714 cells for a 2D mode (a high `points_per_wavelength` with a small `adapt_scale`) was found out by solving it; a convergence check at 0.6 would have made it about 170 000.
4. A material given for `Air*` made `mesh_build` with `physics_sizing` fail ("the sizing names region 'Air*', which the model does not have"): the solver expanded the star, the mesher's wave sizing did not.

The rest (the model turns, the two-model planning, fourteen calls where one script would do) belongs to the host and the agent: `docs/HOST_SETUP.md` and the guide cards say what to do.

## Decision

* **L1, the reader.** `nyx-mcp` reads stdin on a thread of its own. The engine and the script kernel stay on the main thread: a wait is made of slices of 200 ms (`Kernel::wait` with a short wait) and between two slices the server looks at what arrived. A newer `script_run` or `script_wait` ends the wait of the call before it (answered `running`, with a note; the job goes on, the next `script_wait` picks it up); `notifications/cancelled` for the waiting call stops the wait and sends no answer; `ping` and `tools/list` are answered during a wait; a request cancelled before its turn is dropped. Every other message waits for its turn, as before. The printed lines of all slices are kept and a command is counted once.
* **L1, the limit.** A call waits at most `--max-wait` seconds (default 90, 1 to 900). A longer `wait_s` is cut and the answer says `wait_s: {asked, used}`; it is not an error, because an error costs the agent a turn. The tool schema carries the maximum. A call with `_meta.progressToken` gets `notifications/progress` every 5 s.
* **L1, what a `running` answer says.** The job the script waits for: stage, seconds in it, fraction, queue place and the estimate (`Kernel::waiting_job`, `Engine::queue_entry`).
* **L2, noise in a convergence check.** A mode whose `eigenvalue[i].im` is below 1e-9 times its real part on both meshes (a quality factor above 5e8 is not told from rounding) has its `im` row and its quality-factor rows (`Q<n>`, `Q <n> = Re/(2|Im|) of neff`, `f im <n> (Hz)`) marked `noise: true`; they are listed, passed when there is a tolerance and not counted in `worst_relative` or `converged`. The answer lists `noise_modes`. A mode with loss is never noise: a cavity with Q 1e6 has `im/re` 5e-7. Chosen over comparing `im` against the complex magnitude, which would hide a loss figure that does not converge.
* **L3, estimates.** `mesh_build` answers `cost` (cells, dimension, the estimate of a solve of the default chain from the solves this machine has run: seconds, memory, runs, extrapolated; `null` without a basis, no number is invented; a warning above 15 000 cells in 2D and 100 000 in 3D). `convergence_check` takes `dry_run` (both meshes are built, nothing is solved: the cells of each, their cost, the factor between them), `max_cells` and `max_seconds` (refused before any solve, after the finer mesh is built; no refusal on time without an estimate). The finer mesh is built once and solved on, not meshed again.
* **L3, the star.** `Sizing::expand_wildcards`: a name ending in `*` stands for the region and its pieces `name.*` in the label map of the model; a name given in full keeps its own wavelength. Applied where the mesher reads the sizing (`mesh_for_sizing`, `wave_sizes_by_region`).
* **Cards.** `nyx-instructions` (one script per task, `wait_s`, `cost`, `dry_run`), `troubleshooting` (what makes a mesh too large, the noise rows, a loop variable), `optical-modes` (aim `n_target` in a rib guide, the energy fraction in a tensor crystal). The card limit of 3600 bytes holds.

## Not in this decision

* **No estimate from a model of the mesher.** `cost.solve` is null until this machine has solved a few meshes of the same chain and dimension; the history does not yet know the complex solver from the real one, so a fit across both is wide (the answer carries the number of runs and says when it extrapolates).
* **Concurrent tool calls.** A host that sends `api` or `script_check` while a script waits gets them after the wait (at most the limit); only `script_run` and `script_wait` end a wait.
* **A solve is not made faster.** The wait is shorter for the host; the solve takes what it takes.
* **Connecting a host such as Antigravity** (`nyx-connect` has no entry for it) is a separate decision.
decisions.title: The MCP server reads while it waits, and says what a job costs

# 98. Connect knows Antigravity and gives an AI the instructions

Date: 2026-11-20

## Status

Accepted as the latency work L4 (Paul, 2026-11-20: "why cant we have both; that way someone can type into antigravity and it can find the right line; but also people can press connect"). Extends ADR 28 (the one copy of the Connect logic). The number was free after ADR 97.

## Context

Antigravity, where the benchmark session of ADR 97 ran, was not a host of `nyx-connect`: the Connect menu of the app listed only installed hosts, so on a machine with Antigravity and none of the five others it offered "Copy config JSON" and nothing else. The `nyx` entry in Antigravity's configuration had been written by hand and pointed at an older build (the one without the reader and the wait limit of ADR 97), which Connect could not have told the user.

On a machine that runs Antigravity the configuration is `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`, an object `{"mcpServers": {"nyx": {"command", "args"}}}`: the shape Cursor and Windsurf use. Its folder `~/.gemini` is also the folder of Gemini CLI, so it says nothing about Antigravity. A configuration file in the workspace (`.agents/mcp_config.json`) is documented by the vendor and reported as ignored; it is not used.

The command-line program, started by a double click, opened a console that closed at once: with no argument it printed its help and ended.

## Decision

* **A host row.** `antigravity`, name `Antigravity`, file `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` on every operating system, key `mcpServers`, the plain entry (`command`, `args: []`, no `type`). Found by its `config` folder (`~/.gemini/config`), not by `~/.gemini`. Connect, Reconnect (an entry that points at another build is `stale`), Disconnect, the backup and the JSON report work as for the other hosts. `connect_hosts` and `connect_report` go to 1.1 (a host and an enum value added).
* **Instructions an AI can follow.** `nyx_connect::agent_instructions(env, exe)`, shown by `nyx-connect instructions` and by the button "Copy instructions for an AI" of the Connect menu: a text for any AI app that can edit files. It names the program, the entry, the file and the key of every host (this machine's paths, hosts not found marked) and the rules `connect` itself follows: keep the other servers, back the file up once, keep it plain JSON, change only `command` of an existing entry, then say that the app must be restarted. Built from the host table, so it cannot disagree with the rows.
* **A double click is answered.** `nyx-connect` without an argument prints its commands and the state of every host, and on Windows, when it is alone in its console (`GetConsoleProcessList`), waits for Enter. It writes nothing.
* **No `--max-wait` per host.** The entry stays `"args": []`: the default of 90 s is under the 180 s of Antigravity. A host with a shorter limit gets `--max-wait` by hand (`docs/HOST_SETUP.md`).

## Consequences

* Three ways to the same entry: the button, the instructions pasted into the AI app, the snippet by hand. They write the same thing; the row is the only code that edits a file.
* Not tried on a real Antigravity: the file and the entry shape come from a machine that runs it, whether it reloads the file without a restart does not. The text after connecting says "restart or refresh".
* A fifth kind of host (a different shape, a file per workspace) is still one row and one test; nothing in the logic knows the names.
decisions.title: Connect knows Antigravity and gives an AI the instructions

# 99. Figures of modes, and one node order in the results file

Date: 2026-11-20

## Status

Proposed (provisional number: 70 to 79 and 81 are reserved by other plans and the next free number on `main` must be checked at the merge). Built on bookmark `plotting-build`. Follows `docs/PLOTTING_PLAN.md` and `docs/RESULTS_FORMAT_STUDY.md`; amends ADR 62 (layout version 4).

## Context

A script written outside nyx (`plot_sos_mech_modes.py`) drew the modes of a result: `|u|` on the deformed section, arrows of the in-plane motion, the components of a mode, with the phase of each mode fixed by hand. Nothing in nyx could do this without a window, so an assistant or a script could not ask for a picture, and the file layout hid a trap that the script had to find by experiment: the cell fields are stored in the node order of nyx and `/viz/<physics>/cells` in the VTK order, with nothing in the file saying so.

## Decision

* **One node order in the file.** Layout version 4 writes, for each physics, `points` (the coordinates of the nodes) and `cells` (the node of every cell node) in the cell node order of nyx, and says it in the attribute `cell_order` (`v0 v1 v2 e01 e02 e12` for a P2 triangle, `v0 v1 v2 v3 e01 e02 e03 e12 e13 e23` for a P2 tetrahedron, `eij` the midpoint of the edge between vertices i and j). `fields/<name>` is indexed by node, `cell_fields/<name>/{re,im}[c * nloc + a]` is the value at node `cells[c, a]`. A reader gets the nodal complex field without any permutation. Version 3 files are still read. **The `/viz` group is gone** (Paul): it held only a copy of the nodes (identical to `points`) and the cells in another order, 1 to 8 % of a file on seven real files, and no vector copies. **The XDMF file stays** as the light index of the results as stored (Paul: it is for nyx to use the data efficiently, not for ParaView): its Geometry is `/results/<physics>/points`, its Topology `/results/<physics>/cells` with the `Information` element `CellNodeOrder` naming the order, its attributes the stored `fields/<name>` datasets (a vector with its `Components`, shape `[n, m]`). It says in a comment and in an `Information` element `Note` that a viewer such as ParaView must not open it, since it would read the mid-edge nodes in the VTK order and draw them wrongly.
* **Phase, sign and scale of a mode** are an analysis (`nyx_analysis::modeview`, ADR 56): the in-plane components (all but the propagation axis, y in the wafer frame) are rotated by `theta = -1/2 arg(sum u_c^2)` (plain square), then the largest in-plane component at the node of largest in-plane amplitude is made positive, and the peak of `|u|` over the core (the domains asked for, else all) is scaled to 1. The solver's own convention (largest component real, unit modulus) is not changed: it is in the goldens and in the nodal fields. The figure puts every mode in the phase above and reports `quadrature`, the share of the propagation component's energy that is still in `Re` after the phase step. For a guided mode, `d/dy` brings a factor `-iq`, so the propagation component is in quadrature with the in-plane ones when the section has a mirror symmetry along the propagation axis; the number says whether that holds for this mode, it is not assumed. For a real field (a real solver keeps one real amplitude per component) there is no phase and `quadrature` is null.
* **A section** (`nyx_analysis::section`) is the whole mesh of a 2D result, or the face of the cells of a 3D mesh that lies on a plane y = const (the smallest y unless `at` is given). The face of a tetrahedron is a P2 triangle in the native order; P2 triangles are drawn as four linear ones. No interpolation: a plane that no cell face lies on is refused.
* **A figure** is a list of drawing items (`nyx_analysis::canvas`), written as **SVG or PNG**. A field is not a vector drawing: it is rasterised into an image item that the SVG embeds as PNG, while the outline, arrows and text stay vector in the SVG. The PNG is drawn by a small software rasteriser (twice the size, averaged down; text with `ab_glyph` in the font the window carries), with the crates already in the lock file (`png`, `ab_glyph`, `epaint_default_fonts`, `base64`): no system library, no font to install.
* **The command `figure`** (engine, so the window, scripts and the MCP server share it): `physics`, `path` (`.svg` or `.png`), `kind` (`gallery`, `components`), `modes`, `columns`, `cmap`, `warp`, `arrows`, `window`, `at`, `core`, `family`, `panel_width`, `scale`. The reply carries, per mode, the angle the mode was turned by, whether it was flipped, its peak and `quadrature`.
* **No physics is named.** A vector field is found by the names of its cell fields (`<prefix>x`, `<prefix>y`, `<prefix>z`); the title of a mode comes from the label, the frequency scalars and the shares of energy the study wrote (ADR 80); the outline is the border of the section and the edges between cell labels; a displacement (prefix `u`) deforms the section, any other field does not.
* **Where it lives.** In `nyx-analysis` for now (Paul: "analysis is good for now"): no new crate, no new row of the layering table. If the drawing grows (sweep curves, the window drawing the same items), it moves to a crate of its own.

## Measured, and what was found wrong

* On three files of the benches (a 3D Bloch study of a strip, a q = 0 study with absorbing layers, an optical mode study) the figures come out as the script's. The propagation component of the 11 guided modes of the strip is in quadrature to `Re` share 4e-6 to 3e-3; the optical modes to 1e-6. The phase step turns the strip's modes by 0 to 16 degrees (solver convention against the figure's); one mode is turned by 90 degrees and flipped.
* The earlier note that `cell_fields` are "about five times duplicated" was wrong for these files: their meshes are one cell thick, a P2 field has 34980 values per component against 21861 nodes, a factor of 1.6, and the compressed `cell_fields` are 74 % of the file because they carry both parts of three components, not because of duplication. A node-indexed store of continuous cell fields would save at most that factor on these files and is not done.

## Not in this decision

* The window does not draw the figure yet (arrows, the phase of a mode on the screen, a phase animation): the same items can be drawn with egui later.
* Sweep curves (dispersion, mode tracking), the optical next to the mechanical in one figure, scalar results (temperature) and the axisymmetric half plane are not drawn; a result without a vector field is refused with the names it has.
* Nothing of nyx reads the XDMF file yet; it is written, and a test resolves every reference against the .h5. The export reply and the run records list it as before.
* A section inside a 3D mesh, a mesh not periodic along y, a quadrature check for modes with loss or without the mirror symmetry (it reports, it does not correct).

## Consequences

* `engine_commands` gains `figure` (additive, provisional 1.23). The results file is version 4.
* `nyx-analysis` depends on `png`, `ab_glyph`, `epaint_default_fonts` and `base64`.

## Code

`crates/nyx-analysis/src/{section,modeview,canvas,raster,figure}.rs`, `crates/nyx-engine/src/{figure,h5io}.rs`; tests `crates/nyx-engine/tests/{figure,h5}.rs` and the unit tests of the analysis crate.
